Symptoms include restlessness, feeling wound-up or edgy, being easily fatigued, muscle tension, sleep disturbances such as trouble falling or staying asleep, irritability, sweating, nausea, diarrhea, dry mouth, pounding heart/rapid breathing, etc., avoidance behavior, poor concentration, fearful anticipation about future events, inability to relax, unrealistic view of problems, intense craving for immediate solutions, seeing only negative outcomes, perfectionism leading to procrastination due to not wanting to make mistakes, lack of enjoyment despite pleasurable activities once enjoyed, physical signs of stress even when there’s no real danger present. It can be indicative of underlying mental health issues but also may have physiological contributors; hence consulting a professional diagnosis from psychiatrists or clinical psychologists would provide clarity regarding its etiology and management strategies.
reference_answers: An abortion is a procedure to end a pregnancy. It uses medicine or surgery to remove the embryo or fetus and placenta from the uterus. The procedure is done by a licensed health care professional. The decision to end a pregnancy is very personal. If you are thinking of having an abortion, most healthcare providers advise counseling.

Bronchitis is an inflammation of the bronchial tubes, the airways that carry air to your lungs. It causes a cough that often brings up mucus. It can also cause shortness of breath, wheezing, a low fever, and chest tightness. There are two main types of bronchitis: acute and chronic. Most cases of acute bronchitis get better within several days. But your cough can last for several weeks after the infection is gone. The same viruses that cause colds and the flu often cause acute bronchitis. These viruses spread through the air when people cough, or though physical contact (for example, on unwashed hands). Being exposed to tobacco smoke, air pollution, dusts, vapors, and fumes can also cause acute bronchitis. Less often, bacteria can also cause acute bronchitis. To diagnose acute bronchitis, your health care provider will ask about your symptoms and listen to your breathing. You may also have other tests. Treatments include rest, fluids, and aspirin (for adults) or acetaminophen to treat fever. A humidifier or steam can also help. You may need inhaled medicine to open your airways if you are wheezing. Antibiotics won't help if the cause is viral. You may get antibiotics if the cause is bacterial. NIH: National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute

Summary : Adoption brings a child born to other parents into a new family. Birth parents have a number of reasons for placing children for adoption. Overall, they want better lives for their children than they think they can give them. Children who are eligible for adoption come from many different settings. Some are in foster care, a temporary home setting. Other children live in orphanages or with birth relatives until they can be adopted. There are different kinds of adoption. Children may be adopted by a relative or a new family. Some parents adopt children from the U.S, and some adopt from abroad.

After any operation, you'll have some side effects. There is usually some pain with surgery. There may also be swelling and soreness around the area that the surgeon cut. Your surgeon can tell you which side effects to expect. There can also be complications. These are unplanned events linked to the operation. Some complications are infection, too much bleeding, reaction to anesthesia, or accidental injury. Some people have a greater risk of complications because of other medical conditions. Your surgeon can tell you how you might feel and what you will be able to do - or not do - the first few days, weeks, or months after surgery. Some other questions to ask are - How long you will be in the hospital - What kind of supplies, equipment, and help you might need when you go home - When you can go back to work - When it is ok to start exercising again - Are they any other restrictions in your activities Following your surgeon's advice can help you recover as soon as possible. Agency for Healthcare Quality and Research

Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency (AAT deficiency) is an inherited condition that raises your risk for lung and liver disease. Alpha-1 antitrypsin (AAT) is a protein that protects the lungs. The liver makes it. If the AAT proteins aren't the right shape, they get stuck in the liver cells and can't reach the lungs. Symptoms of AAT deficiency include - Shortness of breath and wheezing - Repeated lung infections - Tiredness - Rapid heartbeat upon standing - Vision problems - Weight loss Some people have no symptoms and do not develop complications. Blood tests and genetic tests can tell if you have it. If your lungs are affected, you may also have lung tests. Treatments include medicines, pulmonary rehab, and extra oxygen, if needed. Severe cases may need a lung transplant. Not smoking can prevent or delay lung symptoms. NIH: National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute

Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) is a nervous system disease that attacks nerve cells called neurons in your brain and spinal cord. These neurons transmit messages from your brain and spinal cord to your voluntary muscles - the ones you can control, like in your arms and legs. At first, this causes mild muscle problems. Some people notice - Trouble walking or running - Trouble writing - Speech problems Eventually, you lose your strength and cannot move. When muscles in your chest fail, you cannot breathe. A breathing machine can help, but most people with ALS die from respiratory failure. The disease usually strikes between age 40 and 60. More men than women get it. No one knows what causes ALS. It can run in families, but usually it strikes at random. There is no cure. Medicines can relieve symptoms and, sometimes, prolong survival. NIH: National Institute of Neurological Disorders and Stroke
Summary : Anatomy is the science that studies the structure of the body. On this page, you'll find links to descriptions and pictures of the human body's parts and organ systems from head to toe.

Summary : If you have coronary artery disease, the arteries in your heart are narrowed or blocked by a sticky material called plaque. Angioplasty is a procedure to restore blood flow through the artery. You have angioplasty in a hospital. The doctor threads a thin tube through a blood vessel in the arm or groin up to the involved site in the artery. The tube has a tiny balloon on the end. When the tube is in place, the doctor inflates the balloon to push the plaque outward against the wall of the artery. This widens the artery and restores blood flow. Doctors may use angioplasty to - Reduce chest pain caused by reduced blood flow to the heart - Minimize damage to heart muscle from a heart attack Many people go home the day after angioplasty, and are able to return to work within a week of coming home. NIH: National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute

Anthrax is a disease caused by Bacillus anthracis, a germ that lives in soil. Many people know about it from the 2001 bioterror attacks. In the attacks, someone purposely spread anthrax through the U.S. mail. This killed five people and made 22 sick. Anthrax is rare. It affects animals such as cattle, sheep, and goats more often than people. People can get anthrax from contact with infected animals, wool, meat, or hides. It can cause three forms of disease in people. They are - Cutaneous, which affects the skin. People with cuts or open sores can get it if they touch the bacteria. - Inhalation, which affects the lungs. You can get this if you breathe in spores of the bacteria. - Gastrointestinal, which affects the digestive system. You can get it by eating infected meat. Antibiotics often cure anthrax if it is diagnosed early. But many people don't know they have anthrax until it is too late to treat. A vaccine to prevent anthrax is available for people in the military and others at high risk. NIH: National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases

Fear and anxiety are part of life. You may feel anxious before you take a test or walk down a dark street. This kind of anxiety is useful - it can make you more alert or careful. It usually ends soon after you are out of the situation that caused it. But for millions of people in the United States, the anxiety does not go away, and gets worse over time. They may have chest pains or nightmares. They may even be afraid to leave home. These people have anxiety disorders. Types include - Panic disorder - Obsessive-compulsive disorder - Post-traumatic stress disorder - Phobias - Generalized anxiety disorder Treatment can involve medicines, therapy or both. NIH: National Institute of Mental Health

answers_clean: Acne vulgaris, commonly known as acne or pimples, is a skin condition that occurs when hair follicles become clogged with oil and dead skin cells. It typically affects areas of the body with densely packed sebaceous glands like the face, chest, upper back, and shoulders. The severity ranges from mild to severe cases involving inflammation, redness, swelling, painful nodules, and potential scarring. Hormonal changes during puberty often trigger its development in teenagers but can also occur at any age due to various factors such as stress, dietary habits, medications, genetic predisposition, etc. Treatment options include topical creams/gels containing benzoyl peroxide, salicylic acid, retinoids; antibiotics for bacterial reduction; hormone therapy; Isotretinoin for more severe forms; lifestyle modifications including proper skincare routine and healthier eating patterns may help manage symptoms effectively. Consulting dermatologists helps tailor treatments according to individual needs while minimizing side effects associated with some interventions.

Acute myeloid leukemia (AML) is an aggressive type of cancer that originates in the bone marrow but often quickly moves into the blood as well. It affects immature white blood cells called myeloblasts or blasts which accumulate rapidly due to abnormal growth signals causing impaired production of normal red blood cells, platelets, and mature white blood cells leading to various symptoms like fatigue, increased risk for bleeding/infections etc. Treatment typically involves chemotherapy with possible stem cell transplantation depending upon individual patient factors such age, overall health status & genetic mutations present within their AML subtype.

Adrenal gland disorders include conditions such as Addison's disease, Cushing's syndrome, adrenal cancer, congenital adrenal hyperplasia, pheochromocytoma, primary aldosteronism or Conn’s Syndrome, among others. These can result from overproduction of hormones by one or both adrenal glands or under-functioning due to damage/injury. Treatment depends upon specific diagnosis but may involve medication, lifestyle changes, surgery etc., depending on severity & type of condition.

Yes, alcohol is an addictive substance that can lead to physical dependence when consumed excessively over time. It affects various body systems including neurological functioning which may result in impaired judgment, coordination issues, liver disease (like cirrhosis), cardiovascular problems, gastrointestinal disorders, mental health conditions like depression or anxiety, among others. Moderate consumption might not cause severe harm but chronic misuse poses significant risks for overall well-being. Treatment options include behavioral therapies, medications such as naltrexone, acamprosate, topiramate, etc., along with support groups/programs. Always consult your doctor before starting any treatment regimen. Remember prevention through moderation remains key!

Alzheimer's disease is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder characterized by cognitive decline, memory loss, behavioral changes, and impaired daily functioning due to brain cell damage caused primarily by beta-amyloid plaques and tau tangles in the cortex of the brain. It typically affects individuals over 65 years old but can also occur earlier as early-onset Alzheimer’s disease. Currently, there is no cure for this condition; however, treatments focus on managing symptoms and improving quality of life.

Anal cancer is a rare type of cancer that occurs in the anal canal — the short tube at the end of your rectum through which stool leaves your body. It typically starts with abnormal growths called polyps or lesions inside this area before becoming malignant tumors. The most common form originates from cells lining the inner surface of the anus known as squamous cell carcinoma; other types include adenocarcinomas arising from glandular structures within the wall of the colon. Risk factors for developing anal cancer may involve human papillomavirus (HPV) infection, smoking tobacco products, having multiple sexual partners, engaging in receptive anal intercourse without protection, immune system suppression due to HIV/AIDS treatment medications, chronic inflammation caused by conditions like Crohn's disease or ulcerative colitis, and age over 50 years old. Early detection methods often utilize digital exams performed during routine check-ups along with biopsies if suspicious areas are identified upon examination. Treatment options depend heavily on stage progression but can consistently incorporate surgery, radiation therapy, chemotherapy drugs such as fluorouracil combined with mitoxantrone, targeted theraptaics against specific molecular pathways involved in tumour development, and palliative care measures aim

Anesthesia refers to medications or techniques used during surgical procedures that induce temporary loss of sensation or consciousness in patients for pain relief and comfort while undergoing an operation. There are three main types - general, regional, and local anesthesia. General anesthesia causes total unconsciousness; Regional blocks numb specific areas like spinal cord segments or limbs; Local anesthetics block nerve impulses near small regions such as wounds or dental sites.
"Animal diseases can affect human health through zoonotic transmission when humans come into contact with infected animals or their products."

Yes, antibiotics are medications used to treat bacterial infections by killing or slowing down the growth of harmful bacteria without causing significant damage to host cells. They do not work against viral infections like colds or flu. Misuse can lead to resistance wherein they become less effective over time. Always use them as prescribed by healthcare professionals.

Aphasia is a communication disorder that results from damage to parts of the brain responsible for language production or processing. It can affect speaking, understanding speech, reading, writing, and other forms of expression. The severity varies depending on which areas of the brain have been affected by injury such as stroke, traumatic head wound, tumor, etc., leading individuals with this condition to experience difficulties in expressing themselves verbally or comprehending others' spoken words effectively. There exist different types of aphasias like Broca’s, Wernicke’s, Global, Anomic among others each characterized by distinct symptoms related to specific linguistic functions impaired due to localization of lesion within cerebral cortex involved in language abilities. Treatment typically involves speech-language therapy aimed at improving functional use of remaining capabilities while compensating lost skills through alternative strategies tailored according patient needs & goals alongside supportive care measures addressing emotional wellbeing impacted during recovery process.
answers_noisy: The condition you're describing sounds like acne vulgaris, which is common among teenagers but can affect adults as well. It occurs due to clogged hair follicles from oil (sebum) production in the skin combined with dead skin cells. While generally not serious, severe cases may require treatment by healthcare professionals for scarring prevention and psychological impact management. Maintaining good skincare habits often helps manage mild symptoms effectively.

The condition you're referring to is called Acute Myeloid Leukemia (AML). It occurs when there’s an overproduction of abnormal myeloblasts in the bone marrow which impairs normal hematopoiesis leading to insufficient production of functional red blood cells, platelets, or mature granulocytes needed by body tissues. This can result in symptoms like fatigue due to anaemia, increased risk of bleeding from thrombocytopenia, susceptibility to infections because of neutropenia, as well as other systemic effects depending upon disease progression and individual patient factors. Treatment typically involves chemotherapy with possible stem cell transplantation but outcomes vary widely among individuals.

The small endocrine organ near your kidneys is called an adrenal gland; it can have various disorders such as Addison's disease (adrenal insurighty), Cushing’s syndrome (excess cortisol production), pheochromocytoma (tumor causing excess catecholamines). Symptoms vary but may include fatigue, muscle weakness, mood changes, high blood pressure, weight gain/loss, etc., depending upon which hormones are affected. Always consult with healthcare professionals for accurate diagnosis & treatment options.

Yes, there is extensive information available regarding substances consumed by individuals which can impact health positively (like water for hydration) or negatively (such as alcohol leading to liver damage). It's important always to consult with a healthcare provider before starting new supplements or making significant changes in dietary habits due to potential interactions or side effects.

The condition you're describing sounds like dementia, which includes Alzheimer’s disease as its most common form. It goes beyond typical age-related memory changes; people with this disorder experience significant cognitive decline affecting their daily life activities. Dementia can be caused by various diseases (like vascptaion) but isn't considered part of "normal" aging. Early diagnosis and management strategies may help improve quality of life for those affected. Always consult a doctor if such symptoms arise in yourself or others around you to receive appropriate care and support.

A severe abnormality such as you're describing could be referred to medically as "malignancy" if related to cancerous conditions within reproductive organs (like testicular or ovarian cancers). The implications vary greatly depending upon factors including type of malignancy, stage at diagnosis, overall health status etc., but generally involve treatment options ranging from surgery, chemotherapy, radiation therapy among others with potential impacts on fertility, hormonal balance & sexual functioning along with psychological aspects too. It’s crucial anyone experiencing symptoms consult their doctor promptly for accurate evaluation & management plan tailored specifically towards them.

The substance used by healthcare professionals during certain procedures for pain relief or sedation is called anesthesia. Anesthetics can be administered locally (numbing only part of your body) or generally (making you unconscious). They act primarily by blocking nerve signals in your brain and spinal cord which prevents any sensations from reaching consciousness. There are different types including local, regional, general, intravenous, etc., depending upon the procedure's requirements. Always remember these should never be self-administered due to potential risks involved; they must always be given under professional supervision!

Yes, certain animal-related diseases known as zoonoses can be transmitted to humans through contact with infected animals (pets included). These illnesses may occur due to bites/scratches, handling waste products, consuming contaminated foods, etc. Examples include rabies, salmonellosis, cat scratch disease, ringworm among others. However, not all interactions lead to transmission; proper hygiene practices significantly reduce risks. Regular veterinary care for pets also helps prevent such issues. Always consult professionals if you suspect an issue related to pet ownership impacting human health.

Yes, there is an extensive range of medications used to treat various illnesses including antibiotics such as amoxicillin or azithromycin for bacterial infections; antihistamines like cetirizine for allergies; analgesics (pain relievers) which include acetaminophen and ibuprofen among others; antipyretics also help reduce fever alongside pain relief; antivirals such as oseltamivir can be prescribed during flu outbreaks; insulins manage diabetes by regulating blood sugar levels; statins assist with lowering cholesterol; etc., each tailored according to specific conditions and patient needs under professional guidance. Always consult your doctor before taking new medicine.

Sudden difficulty with speaking (expressive language) or comprehension could indicate an acute neurological event such as stroke; immediate evaluation by emergency services is crucial for proper diagnosis and treatment to minimize potential damage. This condition may involve various areas of the brain responsible for language processing but should be assessed individually through clinical examination and imaging studies if necessary. It's essential to seek urgent medical attention in these cases rather than self-diagnosing.
answers_repaired: Acne is indeed primarily associated with increased oil production from glands at the base of hair follicles that become blocked through accumulation of skin debris such as keratinocytes or bacteria like Propionibacterium acnes. While it commonly occurs around the face, neck, back, shoulders, and chest regions, its presence alone does not necessarily signal broader systemic conditions but may be exacerbated by factors such as stress, dietary habits, medication side effects, endocrine disorders, etc., which could hint towards underlying health concerns requiring further investigation if accompanied by other non-dermatologic signs or persistent despite standard treatments for acne vulgaris typically seen during pubertal development stages.

Chronic Myeloid Leukemia (CML) is a type of cancer that starts from early version cells called stem cells found mainly in the bone marrow. It leads to overproduction of immature granulocytes - a subtype of white blood cells. This can cause symptoms like fatigue, weight loss, night sweats, fever, pain or fullness below rib cage due to enlarged spleen etc., as these dysfunctional WBC crowd out normal ones leading to impaired oxygen transportation, increased risk for infections & bleeding disorders. Treatment often involves targeted therapy drugs such Tyrosine kinase inhibitors which block signals promoting uncontrolled growth; other treatments include chemotherapy, radiation therapy, biological therapies, stem cell transplant depending upon disease stage/progression rate.

Adrenocortical insufficiency is an example of an endocrine disorder that can affect the adrenal glands located above each kidney. Symptoms include fatigue, muscle weakness, loss of appetite, weight loss, abdominal pain, low blood pressure leading to dizziness or fainting upon standing up too quickly, salt craving due to sodium depletion, hyperpigmentation in some cases, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, irritability, anxiety, confusion, joint pains, headaches, mood changes such as depression; decreased sexual desire for both men & women; difficulty concentrating, memory impairments, inflammations/infections throughout body including skin rashes etc.; hypoglycemia which may cause shakiness, sweaty palms, rapid heartbeat, hunger, blurred vision among others. 

Potential long-term effects if left untreated could be severe electrolyte imbalances causing cardiac arrhythmias, shock, organ failure, increased susceptibility to stressors like illness or injury resulting in life threatening Addisonian crisis characterized by sudden penetrating chest pain radiating outward accompanied with shortness of breath, feverish feeling followed rapidly by collapse into coma potentially fatal without immediate treatment through intra

Substances that can be intentionally or unintentionally ingested include foods (nutrients), medications/drugs (prescription, over-the-counter, recreational drugs like alcohol, nicotine from tobacco products) which may have therapeutic effects but also potential for abuse leading to addiction; some household chemicals if mistakenly swallowed due to their availability in homes. Ingestion route of administration affects absorption rate into bloodstream with varying impact depending upon specific properties of each substance such as solubility, pH level etc., potentially causing harmful physiological responses including poisoning symptoms ranging mild gastrointestinal distress up till life threatening conditions requiring immediate emergency care.

The type of progressive memory loss that significantly impacts older adults is Alzheimer's disease (AD). To distinguish AD from normal aging or other forms of dementia, clinicians use criteria such as those outlined in the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders (DSM) which include symptom duration, severity, functional impairments, and exclusion of reversible causes through comprehensive assessment including history taking, physical examination, neuroimaging, laboratory tests, and sometimes genetic testing if there’s suspicion for familial patterns like early-onset cases. Cognitive screenings with tools like MMSE or MoCA help quantify deficits beyond what would be expected due to standard aging processes. Early diagnosis allows timely management strategies aimed at slowing progression and maintaining quality of life.

The term for severe abnormalities or diseases in the lower pelvic area that includes cancers such as prostate, ovarian, cervical, bladder, rectal, etc., is "pelvic malignancies." These disorders significantly impair individuals’ quality of life by causing symptoms ranging from painful urination/defecation to systemic effects due to metastasis; treatment often involves surgery, chemotherapy, radiation therapy which may lead to further complications depending upon disease stage at diagnosis and patient-specific factors.

Anesthesia works by blocking nerve signals to prevent pain sensation or consciousness depending upon whether it's localized (numbing specific areas) or general (inducing unconsciousness). Substances commonly used include propofol for induction of sleepiness; opioids like fentanyl for analgesic effects; muscle relaxants such as rocuronium to facilitate intubation and surgeries requiring immobility; and volatile liquids like sevoflurane that maintain anesthetic depth through inhalation once patients reach operating rooms. Local anesthetics might involve lidocaine which blocks sodium channels temporarily stopping signal transmission along neurons at targeted sites without affecting overall awareness if not combined with other agents mentioned above.
Yes, humans can contract zoonotic diseases from animals or pets which may affect their health significantly if not treated properly. Examples include rabies, Lyme disease, salmonellosis, etc.

The UMLS (Unified Medical Language System) is an extensive database that provides comprehensive terminology coverage of biomedical concepts including diseases, symptoms, diagnoses, body functions or structures related to healthcare services. It includes detailed descriptions, synonyms, relationships between terms, as well as links to other relevant resources such as drug databases like DrugBank which contains data on pharmacokinetics, side effects, interactions, dosage forms etc., making it highly useful when researching treatments for specific conditions. However, please consult with your doctor before starting any new treatment regimen.

Sudden difficulties in speech production (expressive), understanding spoken or written language (receptive), along with reading/writing challenges that occur together suggest conditions like stroke-related Aphasia instead of just Dysarthria which primarily involves muscle control for speech without necessarily impacting cognitive aspects of language processing directly.
reference_answers: Acne is a common skin disease that causes pimples. Pimples form when hair follicles under your skin clog up. Most pimples form on the face, neck, back, chest, and shoulders. Anyone can get acne, but it is common in teenagers and young adults. It is not serious, but it can cause scars. No one knows exactly what causes acne. Hormone changes, such as those during the teenage years and pregnancy, probably play a role. There are many myths about what causes acne. Chocolate and greasy foods are often blamed, but there is little evidence that foods have much effect on acne in most people. Another common myth is that dirty skin causes acne; however, blackheads and pimples are not caused by dirt. Stress doesn't cause acne, but stress can make it worse. If you have acne - Clean your skin gently - Try not to touch your skin - Avoid the sun Treatments for acne include medicines and creams. NIH: National Institute of Arthritis and Musculoskeletal and Skin Diseases

Leukemia is cancer of the white blood cells. White blood cells help your body fight infection. Your blood cells form in your bone marrow. In leukemia, however, the bone marrow produces abnormal white blood cells. These cells crowd out the healthy blood cells, making it hard for blood to do its work. In acute myeloid leukemia (AML), there are too many of a specific type of white blood cell called a myeloblast. AML is the most common type of acute leukemia in adults. This type of cancer usually gets worse quickly if it is not treated. Possible risk factors include smoking, previous chemotherapy treatment, and exposure to radiation. Symptoms of AML include: - Fever - Shortness of breath - Easy bruising or bleeding - Bleeding under the skin - Weakness or feeling tired - Weight loss or loss of appetite Tests that examine the blood and bone marrow diagnose AML. Treatments include chemotherapy, other drugs, radiation therapy, stem cell transplants, and targeted therapy. Targeted therapy uses substances that attack cancer cells without harming normal cells. Once the leukemia is in remission, you need additional treatment to make sure that it does not come back. NIH: National Cancer Institute

The adrenal glands are small glands located on top of each kidney. They produce hormones that you can't live without, including sex hormones and cortisol. Cortisol helps you respond to stress and has many other important functions. With adrenal gland disorders, your glands make too much or not enough hormones. In Cushing's syndrome, there's too much cortisol, while with Addison's disease, there is too little. Some people are born unable to make enough cortisol. Causes of adrenal gland disorders include - Genetic mutations - Tumors including pheochromocytomas - Infections - A problem in another gland, such as the pituitary, which helps to regulate the adrenal gland - Certain medicines Treatment depends on which problem you have. Surgery or medicines can treat many adrenal gland disorders. NIH: National Institute of Child Health and Human Development

Summary : If you are like many Americans, you drink alcohol at least occasionally. For many people, moderate drinking is probably safe. It may even have health benefits, including reducing your risk of certain heart problems. For most women and for most people over 65, moderate drinking is no more than three drinks a day or seven drinks per week. For men under 65, it is no more than four drinks a day or 14 drinks per week. Some people should not drink at all, including alcoholics, children, pregnant women, people taking certain medicines, and people with certain medical conditions. If you have questions about whether it is safe for you to drink, speak with your health care provider. Anything more than moderate drinking can be risky. Heavy drinking can lead to alcoholism and alcohol abuse, as well as injuries, liver disease, heart disease, cancer, and other health problems. It can also cause problems at home, at work, and with friends. NIH: National Institute on Alcohol Abuse and Alcoholism

Alzheimer's disease (AD) is the most common form of dementia among older people. Dementia is a brain disorder that seriously affects a person's ability to carry out daily activities. AD begins slowly. It first involves the parts of the brain that control thought, memory and language. People with AD may have trouble remembering things that happened recently or names of people they know. A related problem, mild cognitive impairment (MCI), causes more memory problems than normal for people of the same age. Many, but not all, people with MCI will develop AD. In AD, over time, symptoms get worse. People may not recognize family members. They may have trouble speaking, reading or writing. They may forget how to brush their teeth or comb their hair. Later on, they may become anxious or aggressive, or wander away from home. Eventually, they need total care. This can cause great stress for family members who must care for them. AD usually begins after age 60. The risk goes up as you get older. Your risk is also higher if a family member has had the disease. No treatment can stop the disease. However, some drugs may help keep symptoms from getting worse for a limited time. NIH: National Institute on Aging

The anus is where stool leaves your body when you go to the bathroom. It is made up of your outer layers of skin and the end of your large intestine. Anal cancer is a disease in which cancer cells form in the tissues of the anus. Anal cancer is rare. It is more common in smokers and people over 50. You are also at higher risk if you have HPV, have anal sex, or have many sexual partners. Symptoms include bleeding, pain, or lumps in the anal area. Anal itching and discharge can also be signs of anal cancer. Doctors use tests that examine the anus to diagnose anal cancer. They include a physical exam, endoscopy, ultrasound, and biopsy. Treatments include radiation therapy, chemotherapy, and surgery. NIH: National Cancer Institute

If you are having surgery, your doctor will give you medicine called an anesthetic. Anesthetics reduce or prevent pain. There are three main types: - Local - numbs one small area of the body. You stay awake and alert. - Regional - blocks pain in an area of the body, such an arm or leg. A common type is epidural anesthesia, which is often used during childbirth. - General - makes you unconscious. You do not feel any pain, and you do not remember the procedure afterwards. You may also get a mild sedative to relax you. You stay awake but may not remember the procedure afterwards. Sedation can be used with or without anesthesia. The type of anesthesia or sedation you get depends on many factors. They include the procedure you are having and your current health.

Animal diseases that people can catch are called zoonoses. Many diseases affecting humans can be traced to animals or animal products. You can get a disease directly from an animal, or indirectly, through the environment. Farm animals can carry diseases. If you touch them or things they have touched, like fencing or buckets, wash your hands thoroughly. Adults should make sure children who visit farms or petting zoos wash up as well. Though they may be cute and cuddly, wild animals may carry germs, viruses, and parasites. Deer and deer mice carry ticks that cause Lyme disease. Some wild animals may carry rabies. Enjoy wildlife from a distance. Pets can also make you sick. Reptiles pose a particular risk. Turtles, snakes and iguanas can transmit Salmonella bacteria to their owners. You can get rabies from an infected dog or toxoplasmosis from handling kitty litter of an infected cat. The chance that your dog or cat will make you sick is small. You can reduce the risk by practicing good hygiene, keeping pet areas clean and keeping your pets' shots up-to-date.

Summary : Antibiotics are powerful medicines that fight bacterial infections. Used properly, antibiotics can save lives. They either kill bacteria or keep them from reproducing. Your body's natural defenses can usually take it from there. Antibiotics do not fight infections caused by viruses, such as - Colds - Flu - Most coughs and bronchitis - Sore throats, unless caused by strep If a virus is making you sick, taking antibiotics may do more harm than good. Using antibiotics when you don't need them, or not using them properly, can add to antibiotic resistance. This happens when bacteria change and become able to resist the effects of an antibiotic. When you take antibiotics, follow the directions carefully. It is important to finish your medicine even if you feel better. If you stop treatment too soon, some bacteria may survive and re-infect you. Do not save antibiotics for later or use someone else's prescription. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention

Aphasia is a disorder caused by damage to the parts of the brain that control language. It can make it hard for you to read, write, and say what you mean to say. It is most common in adults who have had a stroke. Brain tumors, infections, injuries, and dementia can also cause it. The type of problem you have and how bad it is depends on which part of your brain is damaged and how much damage there is. There are four main types: - Expressive aphasia - you know what you want to say, but you have trouble saying or writing what you mean - Receptive aphasia - you hear the voice or see the print, but you can't make sense of the words - Anomic aphasia - you have trouble using the correct word for objects, places, or events - Global aphasia - you can't speak, understand speech, read, or write Some people recover from aphasia without treatment. Most, however, need language therapy as soon as possible. NIH: National Institute of Neurological Disorders and Stroke

answers_clean: Yes, Hemoglobin A1c (HbA1c) is a blood test that measures average levels of glucose in your blood over approximately three months by assessing glycation of hemoglobin molecules within red blood cells. It's commonly used to diagnose diabetes or prediabetes and monitor long-term glucose control in individuals with diabetes. An HbA1c level below 5.7% indicates normal blood sugar regulation; between 5.7% - 6.4% suggests prediabetes, while an HbA1c above 6.5% typically signifies diabetes when confirmed through repeated testing. The American Diabetes Association recommends routine monitoring for people with type 2 diabetes at least twice per year if well controlled, quarterly otherwise. Regular physical activity can help lower HbA1c values along with medication adherence as prescribed by healthcare providers.

An acoustic neuroma, also known as vestibular schwannoma, is a noncancerous tumor that develops on the eighth cranial nerve leading from your inner ear to your brain. The branches of this nerve directly influence hearing and balance functions; hence these types of benign growth can cause issues such as hearing loss or ringing in one's ears, imbalance, dizziness among others if they grow large enough. Treatment options include monitoring for smaller ones, radiation therapy, or surgical removal depending upon its size, location, patient’s age, overall health etc.

Alcoholism, also known as alcohol use disorder or addiction, refers to an inability to manage drinking habits despite adverse social, occupational, physical, emotional consequences of excessive consumption. It involves both psychological dependence—craving for more alcohol due to its pleasurable effects—and physiological tolerance where increasing amounts of alcohol are needed over time to achieve similar intoxication levels. 

Alcohol abuse describes patterns of harmful usage that may not meet all criteria necessary for diagnosing alcoholism but still result in significant impairment or distress. This can include recurrent hazardous situations while under influence such as driving accidents; legal problems related to alcohol misconrights like DUI charges; persistent interpersonal issues stemming from repeated neglected responsibilities at work/home because of prioritizing substances above other obligations etc., which do not necessarily involve dependency symptoms seen with full-blown alcoholism. Both conditions require professional help through counseling, support groups, medications if required, lifestyle changes among others depending upon severity & individual needs.

It typically develops during early childhood when there's an imbalance between two eyes resulting from conditions such as strabismus (misaligned eyes), significant differences in prescription strength between the two eyes, or any obstruction of visual input like cataract. Early detection and treatment can help improve outcomes for individuals affected by amblyopia.

Anal disorders refer to various conditions that affect the anus or rectum such as hemorrhoids, anal fissures, perianal abscesses, itching (pruritus ani), skin tags around the anus, anal incontinence, and more serious diseases like colorectal cancer. They most commonly occur in arteries at various locations such as abdominal aorta, brain's cerebral circulation, legs etc., causing life-threatening internal bleeding when they burst. Risk factors include high blood pressure, smoking, family history among others. Treatment depends upon size, location & risk associated with surgery vs natural progression; may involve monitoring, medications for controlling contributing conditions like hypertension, endovascular procedures or open surgeries.

Symptoms may include fatigue, muscle weakness, loss of appetite, weight loss, low blood sugar levels, nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, darkening of skin areas, increased pigmentation, depression/mood swings, irritability, joint & bone pain, dizziness upon standing up due to orthostatic hypotension etc., potentially leading to an Adrenal Crisis if not treated promptly with emergency care involving IV fluids and steroid replacement therapy. It can be life-threatening but manageable through proper treatment including lifelong medications replacing deficient hormones.

Yes, advance directives (ADs) refer to legal documents that allow individuals to convey their decisions about end-of-life care ahead of time. They provide guidance for healthcare providers when patients become unable to communicate or make informed decisions due to illness or incapacity. There are two main types of ADs - living wills and durable power of attorney for healthcare. Living wills outline specific treatments one wishes to receive or avoid; while Durable Power of Attorney allows another person (a proxy/agent), usually trusted family members or friends, to make treatment decisions if you're unconscious or mentally impaired. These tools ensure your preferences regarding life support measures, pain management, organ donation etc., are respected even during critical situations wherein communication might be impossible. It’s recommended everyone discusses these matters with loved ones & creates such plans as per personal belief systems and values. Always consult local laws since regulations may vary by location.

Common causes include strabismus (misaligned eyes), significant differences in refractive errors among the two eyes, or obstruction from cataracts. If untreated during childhood, this condition can lead to permanent loss of depth perception and binocular vision later in life. Treatments may involve patch therapy over the stronger eye(s) forcing use of the affected eye(s). Early detection through routine pediatric screenings greatly improves outcomes for individuals diagnosed with amblyopia.

reference_answers: Summary : A1C is a blood test for type 2 diabetes and prediabetes. It measures your average blood glucose, or blood sugar, level over the past 3 months. Doctors may use the A1C alone or in combination with other diabetes tests to make a diagnosis. They also use the A1C to see how well you are managing your diabetes. This test is different from the blood sugar checks that people with diabetes do every day. Your A1C test result is given in percentages. The higher the percentage, the higher your blood sugar levels have been: - A normal A1C level is below 5.7 percent - Prediabetes is between 5.7 to 6.4 percent. Having prediabetes is a risk factor for getting type 2 diabetes. People with prediabetes may need retests every year. - Type 2 diabetes is above 6.5 percent - If you have diabetes, you should have the A1C test at least twice a year. The A1C goal for many people with diabetes is below 7. It may be different for you. Ask what your goal should be. If your A1C result is too high, you may need to change your diabetes care plan. NIH: National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases

An acoustic neuroma is a benign tumor that develops on the nerve that connects the ear to the brain. The tumor usually grows slowly. As it grows, it presses against the hearing and balance nerves. At first, you may have no symptoms or mild symptoms. They can include - Loss of hearing on one side - Ringing in ears - Dizziness and balance problems The tumor can also eventually cause numbness or paralysis of the face. If it grows large enough, it can press against the brain, becoming life-threatening. Acoustic neuroma can be difficult to diagnose, because the symptoms are similar to those of middle ear problems. Ear exams, hearing tests, and scans can show if you have it. If the tumor stays small, you may only need to have it checked regularly. If you do need treatment, surgery and radiation are options. If the tumors affect both hearing nerves, it is often because of a genetic disorder called neurofibromatosis. NIH: National Institute on Deafness and Communication Disorders

Your adrenal glands are just above your kidneys. The outside layer of these glands makes hormones that help your body respond to stress and regulate your blood pressure and water and salt balance. Addison disease happens if the adrenal glands don't make enough of these hormones. A problem with your immune system usually causes Addison disease. The immune system mistakenly attacks your own tissues, damaging your adrenal glands. Other causes include infections and cancer. Symptoms include - Weight loss - Muscle weakness - Fatigue that gets worse over time - Low blood pressure - Patchy or dark skin Lab tests can confirm that you have Addison disease. If you don't treat it, it can be fatal. You will need to take hormone pills for the rest of your life. If you have Addison disease, you should carry an emergency ID. It should say that you have the disease, list your medicines and say how much you need in an emergency. NIH: National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases

Summary : What kind of medical care would you want if you were too ill or hurt to express your wishes? Advance directives are legal documents that allow you to spell out your decisions about end-of-life care ahead of time. They give you a way to tell your wishes to family, friends, and health care professionals and to avoid confusion later on. A living will tells which treatments you want if you are dying or permanently unconscious. You can accept or refuse medical care. You might want to include instructions on - The use of dialysis and breathing machines - If you want to be resuscitated if your breathing or heartbeat stops - Tube feeding - Organ or tissue donation A durable power of attorney for health care is a document that names your health care proxy. Your proxy is someone you trust to make health decisions for you if you are unable to do so. NIH: National Cancer Institute

For most adults, moderate alcohol use is probably not harmful. However, about 18 million adult Americans have an alcohol use disorder. This means that their drinking causes distress and harm. It includes alcoholism and alcohol abuse. Alcoholism, or alcohol dependence, is a disease that causes - Craving - a strong need to drink - Loss of control - not being able to stop drinking once you've started - Physical dependence - withdrawal symptoms - Tolerance - the need to drink more alcohol to feel the same effect With alcohol abuse, you are not physically dependent, but you still have a serious problem. The drinking may cause problems at home, work, or school. It may cause you to put yourself in dangerous situations, or lead to legal or social problems. Another common problem is binge drinking. It is drinking about five or more drinks in two hours for men. For women, it is about four or more drinks in two hours. Too much alcohol is dangerous. Heavy drinking can increase the risk of certain cancers. It can cause damage to the liver, brain, and other organs. Drinking during pregnancy can harm your baby. Alcohol also increases the risk of death from car crashes, injuries, homicide, and suicide. If you want to stop drinking, there is help. Start by talking to your health care provider. Treatment may include medicines, counseling, and support groups. NIH: National Institute on Alcohol Abuse and Alcoholism

Amblyopia, or "lazy eye," is the most common cause of visual impairment in children. It happens when an eye fails to work properly with the brain. The eye may look normal, but the brain favors the other eye. In some cases, it can affect both eyes. Causes include - Strabismus - a disorder in which the two eyes don't line up in the same direction - Refractive error in an eye - when one eye cannot focus as well as the other, because of a problem with its shape. This includes nearsightedness, farsightedness, and astigmatism. - Cataract - a clouding in the lens of the eye It can be hard to diagnose amblyopia. It is often found during a routine vision exam. Treatment for amblyopia forces the child to use the eye with weaker vision. There are two common ways to do this. One is to have the child wear a patch over the good eye for several hours each day, over a number of weeks to months. The other is with eye drops that temporarily blur vision. Each day, the child gets a drop of a drug called atropine in the stronger eye. It is also sometimes necessary to treat the underlying cause. This could include glasses or surgery. NIH: National Eye Institute

The anus is the opening of the rectum through which stool passes out of your body. Problems with the anus are common. They include hemorrhoids, abscesses, fissures (cracks), and cancer. You may be embarrassed to talk about your anal troubles. But it is important to let your doctor know, especially if you have pain or bleeding. The more details you can give about your problem, the better your doctor will be able to help you. Treatments vary depending on the particular problem. NIH: National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases

An aneurysm is a bulge or "ballooning" in the wall of an artery. Arteries are blood vessels that carry oxygen-rich blood from the heart to other parts of the body. If an aneurysm grows large, it can burst and cause dangerous bleeding or even death. Most aneurysms occur in the aorta, the main artery that runs from the heart through the chest and abdomen. Aneurysms also can happen in arteries in the brain, heart and other parts of the body. If an aneurysm in the brain bursts, it causes a stroke. Aneurysms can develop and become large before causing any symptoms. Often doctors can stop aneurysms from bursting if they find and treat them early. They use imaging tests to find aneurysms. Often aneurysms are found by chance during tests done for other reasons. Medicines and surgery are the two main treatments for aneurysms. NIH: National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute

Your ankle bone and the ends of your two lower leg bones make up the ankle joint. Your ligaments, which connect bones to one another, stabilize and support it. Your muscles and tendons move it. The most common ankle problems are sprains and fractures. A sprain is an injury to the ligaments. It may take a few weeks to many months to heal completely. A fracture is a break in a bone. You can also injure other parts of the ankle such as tendons, which join muscles to bone, and cartilage, which cushions your joints. Ankle sprains and fractures are common sports injuries.

Summary : Antidepressants are medicines that treat depression. Your doctor can prescribe them for you. They work to balance some of the natural chemicals in our brains. It may take several weeks for them to help. There are several types of antidepressants. You and your doctor may have to try a few before finding what works best for you. Antidepressants may cause mild side effects that usually do not last long. These may include headache, nausea, sleep problems, restlessness, and sexual problems. Tell your doctor if you have any side effects. You should also let your doctor know if you take any other medicines, vitamins, or herbal supplements. It is important to keep taking your medicines, even if you feel better. Do not stop taking your medicines without talking to your doctor. You often need to stop antidepressants gradually. NIH: National Institute of Mental Health

An allergy is an immune system response to substances called allergens that are generally harmless but trigger an allergic reaction in some individuals. These reactions can range from mild symptoms like sneezing or hives to severe life-threatening conditions such as anaphylaxis. Common allergens include pollen, dust mites, pet dander, mold spores, insect stings, certain foods, and medications.

These deposits can occur systemically or locally in specific areas like the heart, kidneys, liver, spleen, nervous tissue, and gastrointestinal tract. There are different types depending on the type of protein involved and its origin within the body.

Anaphylaxis is a severe, potentially life-threatening allergic reaction that occurs rapidly after exposure to an allergen. It can affect multiple organ systems including the skin, respiratory system, cardiovascular system, gastrointestinal tract, and nervous system. Symptoms may include hives, swelling of lips or face, difficulty breathing, rapid heartbeat, nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, dizziness, loss of consciousness, and in extreme cases, death if not treated promptly with epinephrine.

It's often a sign of coronary artery disease where arteries supplying the heart become narrowed or blocked by plaque buildup. There are different types including stable angina, unstable angina, variant (or Prinzmetal’s) angina, and microvascular angina.

Adhesions are bands of scar-like tissue. Normally, internal tissues and organs have slippery surfaces so they can shift easily as the body moves. Adhesions cause tissues and organs to stick together. They might connect the loops of the intestines to each other, to nearby organs, or to the wall of the abdomen. They can pull sections of the intestines out of place. This may block food from passing through the intestine. Adhesions can occur anywhere in the body. But they often form after surgery on the abdomen. Almost everyone who has surgery on the abdomen gets adhesions. Some adhesions don't cause any problems. But when they partly or completely block the intestines, they cause symptoms such as - Severe abdominal pain or cramping - Vomiting - Bloating - An inability to pass gas - Constipation Adhesions can sometimes cause infertility in women by preventing fertilized eggs from reaching the uterus. No tests are available to detect adhesions. Doctors usually find them during surgery to diagnose other problems. Some adhesions go away by themselves. If they partly block your intestines, a diet low in fiber can allow food to move easily through the affected area. If you have a complete intestinal obstruction, it is life threatening. You should get immediate medical attention and may need surgery. NIH: National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases

AS is more common and more severe in men. It often runs in families. The cause is unknown, but it is likely that both genes and factors in the environment play a role. AS has no cure, but medicines can relieve symptoms and may keep the disease from getting worse. Eating a healthy diet, not smoking, and exercising can also help. Bronchitis is an inflammation of the bronchial tubes, the airways that carry air to your lungs. It causes a cough that often brings up mucus. It can also cause shortness of breath, wheezing, a low fever, and chest tightness. There are two main types of bronchitis: acute and chronic. Most cases of acute bronchitis get better within several days. But your cough can last for several weeks after the infection is gone. The same viruses that cause colds and the flu often cause acute bronchitis. These viruses spread through the air when people cough, or though physical contact (for example, on unwashed hands). Leukemia is cancer of the white blood cells. White blood cells help your body fight infection. Your blood cells form in your bone marrow. In leukemia, however, the bone marrow produces abnormal white blood cells. These cells crowd out the healthy blood cells, making it hard for blood to do its work. In acute myeloid leukemia (AML), there are too many of a specific type of white blood cell called a myeloblast. AML is the most common type of acute leukemia in adults. This type of cancer usually gets worse quickly if it is not treated. Possible risk factors include smoking, previous chemotherapy treatment, and exposure to radiation. Once the leukemia is in remission, you need additional treatment to make sure that it does not come back. NIH: National Cancer Institute

Causes range widely including indigestion, gas, constipation, infections, inflammation, blockages, injuries, or more serious issues like appendicitis, ulcers, hernias, or cancers. The nature of abdominal pain—its location, intensity, duration, and associated symptoms—is crucial for diagnosing its cause.

Acupuncture is an ancient form of Chinese medicine that involves inserting thin needles into specific points in the body to balance energy flow (known as qi or chi) and alleviate pain or treat various physical, mental, and emotional conditions. Practitioners target these points to influence bodily functions and promote natural healing. It's used for treating chronic pain, nausea, migraines, anxiety, depression, and other ailments. The practice is generally considered safe when performed by a qualified practitioner using sterile equipment. However, it may not be suitable for everyone; certain health conditions might contraindicate its use. Always consult with a healthcare provider before starting acupuncture treatment.

Adhesions are bands of scar tissue that form between tissues and organs, causing them to stick together. They can occur in any part of the body but are most common within the abdomen and pelvis. Typically, adhesions result from surgery or inflammation due to conditions like endometriosis or infection. Symptoms vary depending on their location; for example, abdominal adhesions may cause chronic pain or bowel obstruction. Treatment often focuses on managing symptoms unless they lead to severe complications requiring surgical intervention.

African Americans face unique health challenges compared to other racial groups in the United States due to various factors including socioeconomic status, access to healthcare, genetic predispositions, and environmental conditions.

Some key points include:

1. **Higher Incidence of Certain Diseases**: African Americans experience higher rates of hypertension (high blood pressure), diabetes, heart disease, stroke, obesity, and certain types of cancer such as breast and prostate cancers when compared with non-Hispanic whites.

2. **Health Disparities**: There is evidence of disparities in treatment outcomes for many diseases among African Americans versus their white counterparts. This can be attributed partly to differences in socio-economic status which affects both lifestyle choices and ability to afford or access quality care.

3. **Genetic Factors**: Some studies suggest that there may also be some genetic components contributing to these health issues within this population group; however, more research needs to be done in this area.

4. **Cultural Considerations**: Cultural beliefs and practices play an important role in how individuals perceive illness and seek out treatments. Understanding cultural nuances helps improve patient-provider communication leading towards better adherence to prescribed therapies.

5. **Access To Healthcare Services**: Limited availability of affordable healthcare services coupled with distrust stemming from historical mistreatment has led to lower utilization rates by members belonging to this community despite having similar symptoms severity levels observed amongst others seeking help elsewhere under comparable circumstances.

Addressing these complex interplays requires multifaceted approaches involving policy changes aimed at reducing economic barriers alongside culturally sensitive educational campaigns

An allergy is an immune system reaction to a substance that is normally harmless, such as pollen, pet dander, or certain foods. When someone with allergies encounters their allergen, their body identifies it as harmful and produces antibodies to fight it off, leading to symptoms like sneezing, itching, rashes, swelling, or in severe cases, anaphylaxis.

Amyloidosis is a group of rare diseases characterized by abnormal deposits of proteins called amyloids in tissues or organs. These protein deposits can disrupt normal function leading to various symptoms depending on where they accumulate. Common sites include the heart, kidneys, liver, spleen, nervous system, and gastrointestinal tract. Treatment often focuses on managing symptoms and addressing underlying causes if known.

Anaphylaxis is a severe, potentially life-threatening allergic reaction that can occur rapidly after exposure to an allergen such as certain foods, medications, or insect stings. It involves multiple body systems including skin, respiratory tract, gastrointestinal system, and cardiovascular system, leading to symptoms like hives, swelling, difficulty breathing, low blood pressure, and in extreme cases, loss of consciousness or death. Immediate treatment with epinephrine is critical for managing this condition.

Angina is chest pain or discomfort that occurs when the heart muscle does not receive enough oxygen-rich blood, often due to coronary artery disease. It's typically described as squeezing, pressure, tightness, or pain in the chest but can also affect other areas like the shoulders, arms, neck, jaw, or back. There are different types of angina including stable, unstable, variant (Prinzmetal’s), and microvascular. Treatment options vary depending on severity and underlying causes but may include medications, lifestyle changes, procedures such as angioplasty, or surgery.

Ankylosing Spondylitis (AS) is a type of arthritis that primarily affects the spine, causing inflammation of the spinal joints which can lead to severe pain and stiffness in the back, neck, and sometimes other joint areas. Over time, this chronic condition may cause new bone formation leading to some sections of the spine fusing together, resulting in reduced flexibility and potential deformity. AS typically starts during late adolescence or early adulthood. It's more common in men than women. Treatment often includes medication, exercise, physical therapy, and in some cases surgery for managing symptoms and preventing complications.

Antioxidants are molecules that help prevent or slow damage to cells caused by free radicals—unstable atoms that can start harmful chain reactions. Free radical formation is linked with aging and diseases such as cancer, heart disease, diabetes, Alzheimer's, Parkinson’s, and others.

Common antioxidants include vitamins C and E, beta-carotene (a form of vitamin A), selenium, lycopene, flavonoids, polyphenols, and more. These substances can be found in various foods like fruits, vegetables, nuts, grains, some meats, poultry, and fish.

Consuming antioxidant-rich foods may support overall health but should not replace prescribed medications for treating specific conditions without consulting healthcare providers. Excessive intake through supplements might cause adverse effects; thus, dietary sources are generally recommended over supplementation unless advised otherwise medically.

reference_answers: Your abdomen extends from below your chest to your groin. Some people call it the stomach, but your abdomen contains many other important organs. Pain in the abdomen can come from any one of them. The pain may start somewhere else, such as your chest. Severe pain doesn't always mean a serious problem. Nor does mild pain mean a problem is not serious. Call your healthcare provider if mild pain lasts a week or more or if you have pain with other symptoms. Get medical help immediately if - You have abdominal pain that is sudden and sharp - You also have pain in your chest, neck or shoulder - You're vomiting blood or have blood in your stool - Your abdomen is stiff, hard and tender to touch - You can't move your bowels, especially if you're also vomiting

Summary : Acupuncture has been practiced in China and other Asian countries for thousands of years. Acupuncture involves stimulating specific points on the body. This is most often done by inserting thin needles through the skin, to cause a change in the physical functions of the body. Research has shown that acupuncture reduces nausea and vomiting after surgery and chemotherapy. It can also relieve pain. Researchers don't fully understand how acupuncture works. It might aid the activity of your body's pain-killing chemicals. It also might affect how you release chemicals that regulate blood pressure and flow. NIH: National Center for Complementary and Integrative Health

Adhesions are bands of scar-like tissue. Normally, internal tissues and organs have slippery surfaces so they can shift easily as the body moves. Adhesions cause tissues and organs to stick together. They might connect the loops of the intestines to each other, to nearby organs, or to the wall of the abdomen. They can pull sections of the intestines out of place. This may block food from passing through the intestine. Adhesions can occur anywhere in the body. But they often form after surgery on the abdomen. Almost everyone who has surgery on the abdomen gets adhesions. Some adhesions don't cause any problems. But when they partly or completely block the intestines, they cause symptoms such as - Severe abdominal pain or cramping - Vomiting - Bloating - An inability to pass gas - Constipation Adhesions can sometimes cause infertility in women by preventing fertilized eggs from reaching the uterus. No tests are available to detect adhesions. Doctors usually find them during surgery to diagnose other problems. Some adhesions go away by themselves. If they partly block your intestines, a diet low in fiber can allow food to move easily through the affected area. If you have a complete intestinal obstruction, it is life threatening. You should get immediate medical attention and may need surgery. NIH: National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases

Summary : Every racial or ethnic group has specific health concerns. Differences in the health of groups can result from - Genetics - Environmental factors - Access to care - Cultural factors On this page, you'll find links to health issues that affect African Americans.

An allergy is a reaction by your immune system to something that does not bother most other people. People who have allergies often are sensitive to more than one thing. Substances that often cause reactions are - Pollen - Dust mites - Mold spores - Pet dander - Food - Insect stings - Medicines Normally, your immune system fights germs. It is your body's defense system. In most allergic reactions, however, it is responding to a false alarm. Genes and the environment probably both play a role. Allergies can cause a variety of symptoms such as a runny nose, sneezing, itching, rashes, swelling, or asthma. Allergies can range from minor to severe. Anaphylaxis is a severe reaction that can be life-threatening. Doctors use skin and blood tests to diagnose allergies. Treatments include medicines, allergy shots, and avoiding the substances that cause the reactions. NIH: National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases

Amyloidosis occurs when abnormal proteins called amyloids build up and form deposits. The deposits can collect in organs such as the kidney and heart. This can cause the organs to become stiff and unable to work the way they should. There are three main types of amyloidosis: - Primary - with no known cause - Secondary - caused by another disease, including some types of cancer - Familial - passed down through genes Symptoms can vary, depending upon which organs are affected. Treatment depends on the type of amyloidosis you have. The goal is to help with symptoms and limit the production of proteins. If another disease is the cause, it needs to be treated.

Anaphylaxis is a serious allergic reaction. It can begin very quickly, and symptoms may be life-threatening. The most common causes are reactions to foods (especially peanuts), medications, and stinging insects. Other causes include exercise and exposure to latex. Sometimes no cause can be found. It can affect many organs: - Skin - itching, hives, redness, swelling - Nose - sneezing, stuffy nose, runny nose - Mouth - itching, swelling of the lips or tongue - Throat - itching, tightness, trouble swallowing, swelling of the back of the throat - Chest - shortness of breath, coughing, wheezing, chest pain or tightness - Heart - weak pulse, passing out, shock - Gastrointestinal tract - vomiting, diarrhea, cramps - Nervous system - dizziness or fainting If someone is having a serious allergic reaction, call 9-1-1. If an auto-injector is available, give the person the injection right away. NIH: National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases

Angina is chest pain or discomfort you feel when there is not enough blood flow to your heart muscle. Your heart muscle needs the oxygen that the blood carries. Angina may feel like pressure or a squeezing pain in your chest. It may feel like indigestion. You may also feel pain in your shoulders, arms, neck, jaw, or back. Angina is a symptom of coronary artery disease (CAD), the most common heart disease. CAD happens when a sticky substance called plaque builds up in the arteries that supply blood to the heart, reducing blood flow. There are three types of angina: - Stable angina is the most common type. It happens when the heart is working harder than usual. Stable angina has a regular pattern. Rest and medicines usually help. - Unstable angina is the most dangerous. It does not follow a pattern and can happen without physical exertion. It does not go away with rest or medicine. It is a sign that you could have a heart attack soon. - Variant angina is rare. It happens when you are resting. Medicines can help. Not all chest pain or discomfort is angina. If you have chest pain, you should see your health care provider. NIH: National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute

Ankylosing spondylitis is a type of arthritis of the spine. It causes inflammation between your vertebrae, which are the bones that make up your spine, and in the joints between your spine and pelvis. In some people, it can affect other joints. AS is more common and more severe in men. It often runs in families. The cause is unknown, but it is likely that both genes and factors in the environment play a role. Early symptoms of AS include back pain and stiffness. These problems often start in late adolescence or early adulthood. Over time, AS can fuse your vertebrae together, limiting movement. Some people have symptoms that come and go. Others have severe, ongoing pain. A diagnosis of AS is based on your medical history and a physical examination. You may also have imaging or blood tests. AS has no cure, but medicines can relieve symptoms and may keep the disease from getting worse. Eating a healthy diet, not smoking, and exercising can also help. In rare cases, you may need surgery to straighten the spine. NIH: National Institute of Arthritis and Musculoskeletal and Skin Disease

Summary : Antioxidants are man-made or natural substances that may prevent or delay some types of cell damage. Antioxidants are found in many foods, including fruits and vegetables. They are also available as dietary supplements. Examples of antioxidants include - Beta-carotene - Lutein - Lycopene - Selenium - Vitamin A - Vitamin C - Vitamin E Vegetables and fruits are rich sources of antioxidants. There is good evidence that eating a diet with lots of vegetables and fruits is healthy and lowers risks of certain diseases. But it isn't clear whether this is because of the antioxidants, something else in the foods, or other factors. High-dose supplements of antioxidants may be linked to health risks in some cases. For example, high doses of beta-carotene may increase the risk of lung cancer in smokers. High doses of vitamin E may increase risks of prostate cancer and one type of stroke. Antioxidant supplements may also interact with some medicines. To minimize risk, tell you of your health care providers about any antioxidants you use. NIH: National Center for Complementary and Integrative Health

reference_answers: An abscess is a pocket of pus. You can get an abscess almost anywhere in your body. When an area of your body becomes infected, your body's immune system tries to fight the infection. White blood cells go to the infected area, collect within the damaged tissue, and cause inflammation. During this process, pus forms. Pus is a mixture of living and dead white blood cells, germs, and dead tissue. Bacteria, viruses, parasites and swallowed objects can all lead to abscesses. Skin abscesses are easy to detect. They are red, raised and painful. Abscesses inside your body may not be obvious and can damage organs, including the brain, lungs and others. Treatments include drainage and antibiotics.

Leukemia is cancer of the white blood cells. White blood cells help your body fight infection. Your blood cells form in your bone marrow. In leukemia, however, the bone marrow produces abnormal white blood cells. These cells crowd out the healthy blood cells, making it hard for blood to do its work. In acute lymphocytic leukemia (ALL), also called acute lymphoblastic leukemia, there are too many of specific types of white blood cells called lymphocytes or lymphoblasts. ALL is the most common type of cancer in children. Possible risk factors for ALL include being male, being white, previous chemotherapy treatment, exposure to radiation, and for adults, being older than 70. Symptoms of ALL include: - Weakness or feeling tired - Fever - Easy bruising or bleeding - Bleeding under the skin - Shortness of breath - Weight loss or loss of appetite - Pain in the bones or stomach - Pain or a feeling of fullness below the ribs - Painless lumps in the neck, underarm, stomach, or groin Tests that examine the blood and bone marrow diagnose ALL. Treatments include chemotherapy, radiation therapy, stem cell transplants, and targeted therapy. Targeted therapy uses substances that attack cancer cells without harming normal cells. Once the leukemia is in remission, you need additional treatment to make sure that it does not come back. NIH: National Cancer Institute

Angioplasty is a procedure used to open narrowed or blocked arteries, typically caused by atherosclerosis (plaque buildup). The procedure you're referring to is likely angioplasty, sometimes also known as percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI). It's used to treat narrowed or blocked arteries in the heart caused by plaque buildup.

Here’s how it generally works:
1. A thin catheter with a deflated balloon at its tip is inserted into one of your major arteries, usually through the groin but occasionally via other sites such as the wrist.
2. The catheter is guided using X-ray imaging until it reaches the blockage site within the artery supplying the heart muscle.
3. Once positioned correctly over the blockage, the doctor inflates the balloon which pushes against the inside wall of the artery, compressing the fatty deposits (plaque) and widening the lumen for improved blood flow.
4. Often, after opening the artery, doctors will place a stent - a small mesh-like device designed to keep the artery propped open long-term.

Angioplasty can be considered significant because while it isn't surgery in the traditional sense requiring large incisions, it does involve entering the body and manipulating internal structures under controlled conditions. Risks include bleeding from insertion points, infection, allergic reactions to contrast dye used during imaging, re-blockages, etc., though serious complications are relatively rare.

It's always important to discuss specific risks and benefits directly with healthcare providers who know individual health histories best before deciding upon treatment options.

2. The catheter is guided to the narrowed artery using X-ray imaging.
3. Once positioned correctly over the blockage, the doctor inflates the balloon to compress the plaque against the arterial wall, widening the passage for blood flow.
4. Often, after dilating the artery, a small mesh tube (stent) may be placed inside the artery to keep it propped open permanently.

Angioplasty is considered a minimally invasive surgical procedure compared to traditional open-heart surgeries like bypass grafting.
